newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Foreigners seen staying away from Slovenia shares.
newsitem.headline: Foreigners seen staying away from Slovenia shares.

text.p: Foreign capital could steer clear of Slovenian shares for months, depressing an already subdued market, unless the central bank eases rules that are deterring investment, analysts said on Thursday.
Last month the Bank of Slovenia blocked international buying when it announced foreign investors had to open special custodian accounts if they wanted to trade in securities.

The move has triggered a drop of over 20 percent in the blue-chip SBI index and, as foreigners bailed out, turnover has all but dried up. At an average 70 million tolars ($0.5 million) a day it is one seventh of volume before the ruling.
"The new regulations have cooled off interest in Slovenian securities," said Fritz Schweiger, head of equity research at Investmentbank Austria in Vienna.

Tanja Petrocnik, a trader with Bank Austria in Ljubljana, forecast share prices could drop by as much as 30 percent in the next few months. By mid-session on Thursday the SBI index was trading 21.11 points up at 1,281.89.
"(Foreign investors) will not come running back as the custodian scheme is too complicated and too expensive," Petrocnik said.

"In the worst case scenario shares could fall to the level we saw at the beginning of September last year when the index was at its all-time low of 892 points," said a bearish Ljubljana-based analyst.
According to complicated Bank of Slovenia regulations banks have to consider money paid into the accounts liabilities which they must balance against assets.
Banks say charges for the new accounts, which will hinge on operation costs, could exceed 10 percent.

"We were ready to open custodian accounts weeks ago but so far no international investor has wanted to sign a contract because of the costs and complexity of the accounts," said Danilo Grasic of Creditanstalt's Slovenian unit.

"The new accounts are too expensive. I expect we will stay away from Slovenia as long as these restrictions remain, unless share prices fall so much that a significant profit can be made despite the extra cost," a Brussels-based institutional investor said.
The central bank's clamp-down came at a time of heightened international interest in Slovenian shares.

The listing last year of some of the biggest newly privatised companies, like drug maker Lek, food producer Droga and trading company Mercator, had brought an influx of foreign money and triggered an 85 percent rally in the SBI between mid-September and early February.

But the flow of foreign investment has all but dried up since then. Analysts forecast just $17 million of new foreign money to the end of the year compared with the $30 million invested in the first six weeks alone.
They said only parliament passing an expected takeover law could bring about a change of heart at the central bank -- and that most probably not before the end of the year.

"The goal of the Bank of Slovenia was to restrict foreign buying. I expect its regulations will change only when parliament passes a law on mergers and acquisitions and a law on cross-border transactions," Bank Austria's Petrocnik said.
